items.question:
A developer relations manager asks Claude to extract speaker information from 20 conference bios and output JSON. The first run returns objects with inconsistent field names — some use `name`, others use `full_name`; some use `title`, others use `role`. The data cannot be imported without manual normalisation.

Which prompt addition would MOST consistently fix this?

options.A: "Output the results as valid JSON."
options.B: "Use this exact schema for every record: {\"name\": string, \"title\": string, \"company\": string, \"session\": string}. Apply it to all 20 bios without variation."
options.C: "Make sure the field names are consistent across all records."
options.D: "Review your output for consistency before returning it."

items.question: An HR business partner needs to explain a new parental leave policy to employees across three groups: new graduates, mid-career employees managing family demands, and senior employees approaching retirement. She asks Claude for "a clear explanation of the policy" and receives a single formal HR document. What prompt change would MOST improve relevance for all three groups?

options.A: "Explain the policy in plain language."
options.B: "Write three versions at different formality levels."
options.C: "Write three versions of the policy explanation — one for early-career employees new to parental benefits, one for employees currently managing caregiving responsibilities, and one for senior employees near retirement. Each: 150 words, plain language, with one concrete example per version."
options.D: "Rewrite the policy for a general audience with varied reading levels."

items.question: A bid management team has refined their executive summary prompt through 12 iterations over six months, saving each version as a separate file. Preparing for a major pursuit, they cannot determine which version performed best. A colleague argues the iterative process itself was flawed. What is the MOST accurate diagnosis?

options.A: The iterative loop failed because 12 iterations is too many for a single prompt; refinement loops should be capped at 5.
options.B: Each iteration changed too many variables simultaneously, making it impossible to isolate which change drove improvement.
options.C: The team should have used a Project instead of iterating the prompt file, because Projects track version history.
options.D: The loop lacked evaluation and version-control discipline — changes were made without recording which produced better outcomes, so the knowledge was never captured.

items.question: A management consultant asks Claude for "a thorough analysis of market entry risks for three regions." The response lists risks with one-sentence explanations per region. She needs each risk covered with evidence, a likelihood assessment, and a mitigation option. What addition to the prompt would MOST reliably produce this depth?

options.A: Provide a written example showing the first risk analysed at the required depth — evidence, likelihood, mitigation — and instruct Claude to apply that structure to all remaining risks.
options.B: Replace "thorough" with "comprehensive and detailed."
options.C: Ask for "at least 500 words per risk."
options.D: Add "Use a formal risk management framework for your analysis."

items.question:
A communications director writes a 400-word prompt to generate a single 100-word product announcement. The prompt specifies required adjectives, prohibited words, sentence structure patterns, tone on a 7-point scale, four mandatory paragraph transitions, and exact punctuation rules. Claude returns an announcement that technically satisfies every specification but reads as stilted and unnatural.

What is the PRIMARY cause?

options.A: The 100-word target was too short for the number of constraints specified.
options.B: Over-specification eliminated every degree of freedom, preventing Claude from making the natural language choices that produce readable prose.
options.C: The prohibited word list conflicted with the required adjective list, forcing awkward substitutions.
options.D: Punctuation specifications are not honoured in prose output — only in code blocks.

items.question:
A product manager needs a Q3 feature roadmap that serves two internal audiences simultaneously: engineering (wants implementation milestones and technical dependencies) and marketing (wants customer-facing benefit descriptions). She asks Claude for a clearly structured roadmap document.

Which format BEST serves both audiences in a single document?

options.A: A continuous prose narrative describing all features in chronological order.
options.B: A flat bulleted list of all features in priority order.
options.C: A document with one heading per feature and two sub-sections per feature: "Engineering milestone" and "Customer benefit."
options.D: Two separate documents — one for engineering and one for marketing — generated in the same prompt.

items.question:
A financial controller sends Claude a 6-section prompt. Sections 1–5 provide background on a quarterly close process; Section 6 asks Claude to "identify the three control gaps most likely to cause a restatement." Claude returns a thorough narrative summary of the quarterly close process without identifying any specific gaps.

Which explanation is MOST precise?

options.A: Claude cannot process structured multi-section prompts without XML delimiters separating the sections.
options.B: The request required financial judgment that Claude declined to provide without explicit authorisation.
options.C: A numbered list format instruction was missing; without it, Claude defaulted to prose summary.
options.D: Five sections of process background established a documentation frame; the analytical task in Section 6 was buried at the end and treated as secondary to the dominant framing.

items.question: A procurement manager asks Claude to produce a vendor evaluation with two components: a structured table of 12 vendors and a separate executive recommendation. Which TWO length-control specifications should she include to serve both components? (Choose TWO)

options.A: "Write the entire document in under 300 words."
options.B: "The vendor table should have exactly 12 rows — one per vendor — with columns: Vendor, Score (1–10), and Rationale (one sentence)."
options.C: "Keep the executive recommendation concise."
options.D: "Write exactly 3 paragraphs for the executive recommendation, each 60–80 words."
options.E: "Limit the response to five minutes of reading time."

items.question:
A regulatory affairs specialist asks Claude to draft a 20-section compliance report. The response ends mid-sentence partway through section 14. She has reviewed sections 1–13 and confirmed they are accurate. She is now planning her next action.

What should she do NEXT?

options.A: In the same conversation, send: "Please continue from where you left off, starting with the remainder of section 14."
options.B: Start a fresh conversation with the full prompt and add: "complete all 20 sections in a single response."
options.C: Ask Claude to summarise sections 1–13 and regenerate the full report from that summary.
options.D: Add all regulatory source documents to a Project knowledge base and re-run the original prompt.

items.question: A marketing director reviews a colleague's prompt before approving it for the team library. Which TWO characteristics indicate the prompt is a kitchen-sink prompt? (Choose TWO)

options.A: The prompt asks Claude to "analyse the campaign data, draft three ad copy variants, recommend a budget reallocation, and create a social media calendar."
options.B: The prompt provides three paragraphs of background context before stating the task.
options.C: The prompt contains four distinct deliverables, each requiring a different output type: data summary, creative copy, a financial recommendation, and a calendar.
options.D: The prompt uses specific numbers: "three variants," "four platforms," "two weeks."
options.E: The prompt includes two example ad copy pieces as style references.

items.question: A compliance officer builds a prompt template for generating regulatory filings. Which TWO situations justify keeping a negative constraint rather than converting it to a positive instruction? (Choose TWO)

options.A: The output tends to be too long — the constraint is "do not exceed 800 words."
options.B: A specific phrase is legally prohibited in this jurisdiction and must never appear in any filing.
options.C: The tone is too formal — the constraint is "do not use legal jargon."
options.D: A competitor's name must never be mentioned in a regulatory filing under company policy.
options.E: The structure is inconsistent — the constraint is "do not use bullet points."

items.question: An internal consulting team is building a prompt template library for stakeholder update emails. Which TWO practices make the template MOST effective and maintainable for all team members? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Use descriptive placeholder names — {{stakeholder_name}}, {{project_status}}, {{key_risk}} — rather than generic labels like {{var1}} or {{field_a}}.
options.B: Embed every possible scenario and conditional variation directly in the template so team members never need to customise it.
options.C: Include a brief annotation beside each placeholder explaining what value is expected and any formatting requirement, so any team member can substitute correctly.
options.D: Encrypt the template file so that only approved users can read the placeholder logic.
options.E: Generate a separate template version for each stakeholder type so the base template is never modified.

items.question:
A customer success manager asks Claude to write a weekly update she will paste into a plain-text email client that does not render markdown. Her prompt says: "Format the response with headers and bullet points." The email arrives with pound signs, asterisks, and hyphens cluttering the text throughout.

What should she change in her next prompt?

options.A: Ask Claude to use HTML formatting instead of markdown.
options.B: Specify "no formatting" so all structure is removed.
options.C: Specify: "Plain text only — no markdown symbols. Use ALL-CAPS labels for section names and a dash-space prefix for list items."
options.D: Switch to the Claude.ai desktop app, which exports plain text natively.

items.question:
A bid manager adds "Keep the response under 500 words" to the end of a 300-word prompt that contains extensive task detail about a complex RFP. Claude consistently returns 900-word responses across two attempts. She suspects the word count instruction is being ignored.

What is the MOST likely cause?

options.A: 500 words is below Claude's minimum response length for complex prompts.
options.B: The word count instruction conflicted with an implied thoroughness expectation from the task detail.
options.C: Word count instructions are only reliable when placed at the very beginning of a prompt.
options.D: The extensive task detail established a strong generation frame before the constraint was stated; placing the word count limit at the start of the prompt or in a dedicated constraints block would improve compliance.

items.question: A technical writer asks Claude to document a new API: "Write developer-facing API documentation — don't oversimplify." The output is dense and implementation-heavy, suited for senior engineers rather than the intermediate developers who are the actual audience. What went wrong?

options.A: "Don't oversimplify" is too broad — it excluded accessible explanations across the whole spectrum, and Claude compensated by maximising technical depth rather than hitting the middle register.
options.B: Claude defaulted to the highest technical register because the subject was explicitly labelled an API.
options.C: The prompt needed a role instruction to calibrate tone: "You are a technical writer for experienced engineers."
options.D: API documentation always requires expert-level language; a simplification pass should be applied in a second prompt.

items.question: A marketing manager has refined a product tagline across five turns. Each turn produces an objectively more polished version, and the manager approves each step. After turn 5 the tagline is elegant and grammatically refined but has drifted far from the original brand brief. What is the PRIMARY failure mode?

options.A: Five refinement turns exceeded the optimal depth for creative iteration.
options.B: Each turn reinforced incremental surface polish without checking alignment with the original brief, causing the loop to converge on a polished but off-brand output.
options.C: Claude learned the manager's approval pattern and began optimising for approval signals rather than brand fit.
options.D: The conversation history created continuity pressure that prevented Claude from generating alternatives sufficiently different from prior turns.

items.question:
A recruiter uses a prompt template: "Write a personalised outreach email for {{candidate_name}} applying for the {{role_title}} position." A junior team member sends the template to Claude with `{{role_title}}` left unfilled.

What will MOST likely happen?

options.A: Claude will refuse to process the prompt because of the undefined placeholder.
options.B: Claude will pause and ask the user to fill in the missing variable before generating a response.
options.C: Claude will treat `{{role_title}}` as literal text, either including it verbatim in the output or substituting a generic placeholder term.
options.D: Claude will search the conversation history for a previously mentioned role title and substitute it automatically.

items.question: A content team has added new instructions to their Claude Project every week for three months, now totalling 45 separate instructions covering tone, length, format, prohibited words, required sections, citation style, and audience calibration. Content quality has become inconsistent, and guidelines that have been in the project for months are being violated. What is the MOST likely cause?

options.A: The project has reached its instruction character limit, causing the oldest instructions to be silently dropped.
options.B: Some newer instructions were written by team members who did not read the existing ones, creating duplicates.
options.C: Instructions added later always override earlier instructions in the same project, suppressing the original standards.
options.D: 45 competing instructions create a high probability of implicit conflicts and attention dilution; Claude cannot reliably satisfy all constraints simultaneously, making compliance with any individual instruction inconsistent.

items.question: A compliance analyst is reviewing 15 vendor contracts one by one with Claude in a single conversation. In turn 1 she specified: "Flag only clauses that violate our indemnity policy, which requires mutual indemnification." By turn 9, Claude is flagging generally unusual clauses that are not related to indemnity. What is the PRIMARY cause?

options.A: As the conversation grows and each contract review adds new content, the indemnity-specific constraint from turn 1 receives proportionally less attention, causing drift toward general clause flagging.
options.B: Claude applied the indemnity rule to the first eight contracts and then internally reset its review criteria for subsequent ones.
options.C: General unusual-clause flagging is Claude's default review behaviour that re-emerges whenever specific instructions are not repeated in every turn.
options.D: The later contracts contained clause types outside the scope of Claude's training on indemnity requirements.

items.question:
A data analyst asks Claude to extract 50 product records from a catalogue document and output them as JSON. She specified "output as JSON objects." Records 1–20 are clean and consistent, but records 21–50 introduce new field names because those source entries had additional attributes. The resulting JSON cannot be imported without normalisation.

Which prompt change would MOST reliably prevent this?

options.A: "Make sure all records are consistent."
options.B: "Use this exact schema for every record regardless of source attributes: {\"product_id\": string, \"name\": string, \"category\": string, \"price\": number, \"description\": string}. Use null for any field absent in the source."
options.C: "Review your output for field consistency before returning it."
options.D: "Output all records with the same number of fields."

items.question: A developer configures an API call with a system prompt: "Respond only in formal English." She prefills the assistant turn with "Voilà —" — a French exclamation. Despite the system prompt, the full response continues in French. What BEST explains this behaviour?

options.A: Prefilling always overrides system prompt instructions for language.
options.B: The system prompt's language instruction was malformed, causing it to be ignored.
options.C: The French opening token established a language frame at the generation frontier; Claude continued in French because the immediate local context (the prefill) outweighed the more distant system prompt instruction for subsequent token prediction.
options.D: The fix is a negative system prompt instruction — "never respond in French" — rather than the positive instruction "respond in formal English."

items.question: A financial analyst correctly decomposes a bundled prompt into three chained tasks: (1) extract key metrics from the earnings report, (2) compare metrics to prior quarter, (3) draft an executive summary. Tasks 1 and 2 succeed. Task 3 produces a generic, template-like executive summary that mentions no specific figures. What is the MOST likely cause of task 3's failure?

options.A: Task 3 required stronger writing capability; it should have been run on Opus.
options.B: Three chained tasks is still too many; tasks 1 and 2 should have been merged into one.
options.C: Task 3 was run in a new conversation without access to the specific metrics from tasks 1 and 2.
options.D: The prompt for task 3 did not include the specific outputs of tasks 1 and 2 as context; Claude drafted a summary without the data it was supposed to summarise.

items.question:
A UX writer has been refining a single tooltip message with Claude for seven turns. Each turn produces a slightly different version — different word order, synonyms — but no version since turn 3 is clearly superior to any other. A colleague suggests the writer should have stopped several turns earlier.

What principle does this situation illustrate?

options.A: Iterative refinement has diminishing returns; once quality plateaus and no turn produces a clearly superior output, further refinement adds effort without improvement.
options.B: Refinement loops for copywriting tasks should be capped at a maximum of five turns.
options.C: Refinement should only continue if each turn produces a measurably better output as validated against a pre-defined rubric.
options.D: The writer should have switched to a different model tier at turn 4 to introduce more variation.

items.question: A financial services associate asks Claude to review and risk-flag 30 client account notes. The response ends at account 24 with no error message, no indication of incompleteness, and no trailing text. The associate reviews only the 24 accounts covered, missing 6. What failure pattern does this represent?

options.A: Claude applied an internal privacy limit that caps account reviews at 24 per response.
options.B: The response was silently truncated at an output length limit; without an end-of-list marker or count confirmation, the truncation was invisible to a non-vigilant reviewer.
options.C: Six accounts did not contain sufficient information for risk flagging and were silently skipped.
options.D: The original prompt was ambiguous about whether all 30 accounts required individual flags.

items.question: A management consultant's project instruction states: "Always respond in flowing prose — no bullet points." A per-chat prompt for a four-option strategic comparison ends with: "Present the comparison as a 2×4 decision matrix table." Claude returns a prose description of what the table would contain rather than rendering the table itself. What is the BEST explanation?

options.A: Markdown table rendering requires the API; the Claude.ai UI always falls back to prose descriptions.
options.B: The per-chat prompt was ambiguous; "decision matrix" could mean a table or a structured prose comparison.
options.C: The project instruction prohibiting bullet points was interpreted broadly to exclude all non-prose formatting including tables; Claude produced a prose description as a compromise.
options.D: Tables cannot be generated when a format conflict exists; Claude defaults to prose in all conflict scenarios.

items.question: An editorial manager asks Claude to "write in our company's voice — confident, direct, and slightly irreverent." After three separate runs the output is professional and direct but entirely lacks the brand's distinctive irreverence. The manager has tried variations of the same descriptor words. What should she do differently?

options.A: Add more adjectives to describe the irreverent quality: "witty, edgy, cheeky, and self-aware."
options.B: Define "irreverence" explicitly in the prompt before requesting the output.
options.C: Ask Claude to study the brand's social media feeds before writing.
options.D: Include two or three short examples of existing brand copy that demonstrate the irreverent voice; let the examples show what repeated description alone cannot convey.

items.question: A proposal team at a professional services firm uses a prompt template created 14 months ago. The template covers the firm's service portfolio, but three new service lines have been added since it was created. Recent proposals generated from the template omit the new services. What is the PRIMARY cause?

options.A: The template was not updated to reference the new service lines, so the prompt cannot instruct Claude to include what it has not been told to include.
options.B: Claude's training data does not include the firm's new service lines, so it cannot describe them.
options.C: Prompt templates automatically expire after 12 months in Claude Projects.
options.D: New service lines must be added to a Project knowledge base before they can be referenced in any prompt.

items.question: A communications team lead reviews two recent Claude outputs. Which TWO situations represent format failures caused by an under-specified prompt rather than a model capability issue? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Claude returned a 2,000-word report when asked for a "comprehensive overview" and the user wanted 500 words.
options.B: Claude used markdown headers in an output that was pasted into a plain-text system, producing visible symbols throughout the document.
options.C: Claude wrote in a formal tone when asked for a "professional style."
options.D: Claude returned a numbered list when the prompt said "organise the data clearly" but the user needed a table.
options.E: Claude added a one-sentence disclaimer at the end of a legal analysis.

items.question:
A bid manager is refining a value proposition statement. At turn 3 it was at roughly 80% of the target quality. After two more turns, it is now at 60% — each instruction fixed one element but introduced a new problem. She is 5 turns in and the output is worse than at turn 3.

What should she do NEXT?

options.A: Continue adding more specific instructions to patch each newly introduced problem in sequence.
options.B: Switch to Opus to handle the competing constraints with stronger reasoning.
options.C: Stop iterating; return to the turn 3 output and start a fresh conversation with it as the baseline, adding a single consolidated instruction that addresses all remaining gaps.
options.D: Ask Claude to review the current output against the original brief and self-correct without further instruction.

items.question: A senior analyst notices that Claude's outputs in long working sessions become less focused and consistent as the conversation grows. Which TWO mechanisms MOST directly cause this degradation? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Early instructions receive proportionally less attention as the context window fills with later content, causing constraints stated early to lose influence.
options.B: Claude actively deprioritises instructions that have been repeated more than three times in a conversation.
options.C: Per-turn instructions accumulate and may implicitly conflict with each other, creating unresolvable competing requirements that reduce output consistency.
options.D: The model's reasoning capability decreases monotonically with conversation length.
options.E: Longer conversations trigger an internal safety mode that makes Claude more cautious and hedged.

items.question: A strategy consultant bundles five distinct analysis tasks into a single prompt and receives shallow output across all five tasks. Which TWO are the MOST direct consequences of the kitchen-sink structure that explain the shallow output? (Choose TWO)

options.A: The total token budget was insufficient for five tasks combined, causing each task to be truncated.
options.B: Generation capacity and attention were divided across five tasks simultaneously, preventing deep execution on any single task.
options.C: Claude applied an internal per-task length cap when it detected multiple tasks in a single prompt.
options.D: Claude could not apply a consistent analytical frame across tasks with different output types and success criteria, causing each task to be processed superficially.
options.E: The five tasks shared contextual information that created circular dependencies in Claude's reasoning.

items.question: A policy analyst consistently receives outputs longer than specified, even after adding word count instructions to her prompts. Which TWO patterns in her prompts are MOST likely causing the word count instructions to be ignored? (Choose TWO)

options.A: The word count instruction appears at the very end of a long prompt, after extensive task detail that has already established a generation frame before the constraint is reached.
options.B: She uses approximate targets — "approximately 400 words" — instead of exact targets — "exactly 400 words."
options.C: She uses vague qualifiers — "brief," "concise" — without any numeric target, making the constraint unmeasurable.
options.D: She does not repeat the word count instruction in every paragraph of the prompt.
options.E: She is using the web app instead of the API, which does not enforce word count instructions in the same way.

items.question:
A content operations lead at a telecoms company asks Claude to generate 10 social media posts for a product launch. Without format guidance, results have been inconsistent: some posts are too long, some use hashtags, some do not, some include emoji, some do not. She wants all 10 standardised for her social media scheduling tool.

What single prompt addition would MOST standardise output across all 10 posts?

options.A: "Write 10 social media posts about the product launch."
options.B: "Make the posts consistent with each other."
options.C: "Use a professional tone for all posts."
options.D: "Each post: exactly 240 characters, end with 2–3 relevant hashtags, no emoji, active voice. Apply this format to all 10 posts."

items.question: A strategy analyst correctly decomposes a 5-task bundled prompt into 5 separate prompts. The first individual prompt — "Analyse the competitive positioning of three firms" — returns a 2,500-word essay when she needed a 500-word briefing note. What does this reveal?

options.A: Decomposition alone is insufficient — each individual task also needs its own format and length specification; the kitchen-sink was fixed but the under-specification problem transferred to each decomposed task.
options.B: 500 words is too short for a three-firm competitive analysis; the length expectation needs revision.
options.C: The task requires further decomposition — one prompt per firm rather than all three together.
options.D: A word count instruction should have been in the original bundled prompt; decomposition was premature.

items.question:
A developer at a fintech firm is building an API-based workflow that generates investment risk summaries. Each summary must begin with a structured header: `RISK LEVEL: [High/Medium/Low] | ASSET CLASS: [type]`. Without this header, the downstream parser fails. She has tried format instructions but the header appears inconsistently.

Which technique combination would MOST reliably produce the required opening?

options.A: A format instruction alone: "Begin every response with the risk level and asset class header."
options.B: A template variable for asset class in the user message, combined with a prefilled assistant turn starting with `RISK LEVEL:` to mechanically commit the opening structure.
options.C: A post-generation validation step that inserts the header if it is absent.
options.D: A project-level instruction defining the required header format for all responses.

items.question: A bid manager has refined her executive summary template with positive tone instructions across four iterations: "concise," "outcome-focused," "client-centric," and "compelling." After four attempts the summaries remain generic and formula-following. What should she try NEXT?

options.A: Add two more adjectives to the instruction: "strategic" and "differentiating."
options.B: Replace all adjectives with a single negative constraint: "not generic."
options.C: Add two examples of excellent executive summaries from past winning bids and instruct Claude to match their quality, specificity, and energy.
options.D: Move the tone instruction from the template to a Project-level instruction.

items.question:
A procurement analyst has been reviewing vendor contracts with Claude for 12 turns. In turn 12 she writes several paragraphs summarising the review so far, then ends with: "...and could you also flag any clauses that violate our GDPR data processing requirements?" Claude continues the general contract discussion without flagging any GDPR clauses.

Which COMBINATION of problems MOST likely explains this outcome?

options.A: The GDPR flagging task requires a separate project with the GDPR policy documents uploaded.
options.B: Claude lacks knowledge of GDPR requirements and could not assess clause compliance.
options.C: The analyst needed to paste the GDPR requirements explicitly rather than naming the regulation.
options.D: The GDPR task was buried at the end of a long turn AND competed with 11 prior turns of general contract review context that dominated the active generation frame.

items.question:
A legal operations director is designing a master prompt template for 15 lawyers across M&A and employment law matters. M&A outputs need a risk matrix; employment outputs need a narrative summary. She wants a single template that enforces consistent quality while accommodating both practice areas.

What is the BEST structural approach?

options.A: Include a practice area variable — {{matter_type: M&A | employment}} — and a conditional output format section specifying the risk matrix for M&A and the narrative for employment, with an instruction that only one section applies per use.
options.B: Create two separate templates and train lawyers to select the correct one per matter.
options.C: Write both output format requirements into the template and instruct Claude to "use the appropriate format for the matter type."
options.D: Use a project instruction to set a default output format and let lawyers override it per chat.

items.question:
A product marketing manager asks Claude in a single prompt to: (1) generate a feature comparison table and (2) write a narrative blog post about the same features. The response alternates between prose and table format, producing a hybrid that is neither a clean table nor a coherent blog post.

What does this MOST directly demonstrate?

options.A: Claude cannot produce both a table and prose within a single response.
options.B: Bundling tasks with incompatible output formats into one prompt causes Claude to blend the formats, satisfying neither — decomposing into two separate prompts would allow each task to produce its intended format cleanly.
options.C: The table should have been generated first; the blog post prompt should then reference it as source material.
options.D: The prompt needed an explicit section header between the two requested outputs.

items.question:
A compliance analyst receives outputs where every paragraph begins with "It is important to note that..." — a filler opener she wants eliminated. She has added "Don't use filler phrases" to her prompt twice with no improvement.

What is the MOST effective next step?

options.A: Add "Don't use filler phrases" to the Project instruction so it applies to all conversations.
options.B: Switch to Opus — the mid-tier model is more prone to filler openers than the top tier.
options.C: Replace the vague prohibition with a specific one: "Never begin a paragraph with 'It is important to note that' or any similar introductory qualifier. Start each paragraph directly with the substantive finding."
options.D: Prefill the assistant turn with the first substantive word to bypass the filler opener.

items.question:
A marketing team has refined a press release prompt through 8 iterations over 6 weeks. Version 8 consistently produces high-quality press releases. The team lead declares the iteration complete. A senior manager asks what the right NEXT step is to make the quality gains durable and usable by the full team of 12.

What is the MOST appropriate response?

options.A: Archive the full conversation history so team members can reference the iterative reasoning steps that led to version 8.
options.B: Promote the version 8 prompt to a Project-level instruction so all chats in the project inherit its logic.
options.C: Share the version 8 prompt informally via email so team members can copy and modify it.
options.D: Formalise version 8 as a named, documented template with clear placeholders for variable elements, store it in the team's shared template library, and establish a process for future updates.

items.question:
A grant writer drafting a project narrative for a foundation application needs a 3-page deliverable. She prompts Claude for "a comprehensive and deeply detailed narrative of the project's methodology, outcomes, and evaluation framework." Claude returns 12 pages of thorough content. She cannot use it as-is.

What is the ONE-STEP fix?

options.A: "Write a 3-page project narrative (~900 words) covering methodology, outcomes, and evaluation framework — prioritise the most distinctive aspects and omit supporting rationale."
options.B: Specify page count, word count, and section count together to constrain both length and depth simultaneously.
options.C: Remove "comprehensive" or "deeply detailed" — having both establishes a conflicting depth signal.
options.D: Draft a full version and then ask Claude to cut it to 3 pages in a second prompt.

items.question: An HR team has a Project instruction: "All outputs must use UK English spelling." Their job description template uses American spelling in its example sections. New job descriptions are being produced with mixed spelling throughout. What is the MOST efficient fix?

options.A: Delete the project instruction and embed the UK English rule directly in the template.
options.B: Update the template's example sections to use UK English, making the template and project instruction consistent.
options.C: Create a separate project configured without the UK English instruction for job description work.
options.D: Add an explicit override in each chat: "Use UK English for all spelling throughout this response."

items.question:
A financial analyst is two hours into a complex quarterly review session at 35 turns. Outputs have become less precise, and recent responses contradict the agreed framework established in turns 1–5. She must complete the remaining analysis but cannot restart from scratch.

What is the BEST strategy?

options.A: Add a framework reminder to the start of every subsequent prompt to counteract the drift.
options.B: Ask Claude to recall the framework from turns 1–5 by referencing those turn numbers explicitly.
options.C: In the current conversation, ask Claude to produce a clean summary of the agreed framework; start a new conversation with that summary as the opening context for the remaining analysis.
options.D: Switch to Opus for the remaining turns to restore consistency and precision.

items.question:
A regulatory affairs director at a pharma company needs a document serving three audiences: (1) clinical team — 2-page technical summary with data tables; (2) legal team — 1-page risk narrative; (3) executive team — one-paragraph strategic recommendation. Her prompt asks for "a comprehensive regulatory review document." Claude returns a 15-page technical report.

Which prompt structure would MOST precisely produce all three required components?

options.A: "Write a comprehensive regulatory review with clearly labelled sections for clinical, legal, and executive audiences."
options.B: "Write three separate documents — one for clinical, one for legal, one for executives — each at the appropriate length."
options.C: "Write a regulatory review document with three audience-specific sections, each at the appropriate depth."
options.D:
"Write a single document with three named sections:
**Clinical Summary**: 2 pages, include data tables, technical depth appropriate for clinical scientists.
**Legal Risk Narrative**: 1 page, flowing prose, focus on regulatory exposure and liability.
**Executive Recommendation**: 1 paragraph, strategic framing only, no technical detail.
Each section is self-contained."

items.question: A business analyst reviews a colleague's prompt and identifies two problems: (1) the main task is buried in the fourth paragraph after three paragraphs of background; (2) the prompt asks Claude to "be detailed, concise, comprehensive, and brief." What is the MOST complete remediation?

options.A: Move the task statement to the first sentence; replace the contradictory qualifiers with a single positive specification: a word count and a named scope.
options.B: Remove the background paragraphs entirely so the task appears first by default.
options.C: Replace both "detailed" and "comprehensive" with a word count instruction, leaving the task in its current position.
options.D: Add a section header "Task:" before the task statement and remove the conflicting qualifiers.

items.question:
An internal auditor writes a prompt: three paragraphs describing a vendor risk scenario, then ending with "...and could you perhaps let me know what you think?" Claude returns a general commentary on vendor risk management. She needed a structured risk register with columns: Risk, Likelihood (H/M/L), Impact (H/M/L), and Mitigation Control.

Which revision addresses ALL identified problems in one step?

options.A: Remove the politeness padding and add the risk register format at the end of the existing prompt.
options.B: "Produce a risk register with columns: Risk, Likelihood (H/M/L), Impact (H/M/L), and Mitigation Control. Source the risks from the following vendor scenario: [scenario text]"
options.C: Ask Claude in a follow-up turn to reformat the commentary as a risk register.
options.D: Add a section header "Deliverable:" before the format request at the end of the current prompt.

items.question: A communications manager asks Claude to write 5 product announcement emails — one per customer segment — in a single prompt. She receives 5 generic emails with identical structure and no segment-specific messaging. Which TWO changes TOGETHER would MOST effectively produce differentiated, segment-specific emails? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Switch to Opus for stronger segment differentiation capability.
options.B: Add "Be segment-specific" to the existing bundled prompt.
options.C: Write one prompt per segment so each prompt can establish a clear single-audience frame.
options.D: For each segment prompt, provide the segment's specific characteristics, primary concerns, and preferred communication register explicitly.
options.E: Ask Claude to review the 5 generic emails and differentiate them in a follow-up turn.

items.question:
A bid manager identifies three problems in her capability statement prompt: (1) output is 800 words when 300 are needed; (2) the capability statement task appears after 200 words of company background — the main deliverable is buried; (3) the tone instruction "professional but approachable" consistently produces stiff, formal text across three runs. She must fix all three in a single revised prompt.

What approach would MOST effectively address all three in one revision?

options.A: Open the revised prompt with the task and word count: "Write a 300-word capability statement"; follow with a positive tone instruction anchored by an example sentence demonstrating the desired register; then provide the company background as context.
options.B: Fix tone first (add more adjectives), then fix length (add the word count), then fix the buried ask (add a section header) — three sequential targeted changes to the existing prompt.
options.C: Fix the length first by inserting "300 words" into the existing prompt; address the structure and tone in two follow-up refinement turns.
options.D: Restructure the prompt by moving the task and background to match their current order but add a word count, a tone adjective, and a section header.

items.question: A consulting firm is designing a proposal template for 50 consultants across 8 practice areas. The managing director wants consistent quality standards while allowing practice-specific customisation. Which TWO template design choices BEST balance these goals? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Lock every element of the template so no customisation is possible.
options.B: Use named placeholder variables for practice-specific elements — {{practice_area}}, {{primary_service}}, {{relevant_case_study}} — while keeping quality instructions, format, and tone as fixed template text.
options.C: Add a "Practice area notes" section at the end of the template where practice leads document their specific context, providing Claude with relevant differentiation information per engagement.
options.D: Create a separate template for each of the 8 practice areas with no shared elements.
options.E: Allow consultants to freely modify the template's instruction text in addition to substituting variables.
